chapters.title: Chapter 1: Foundations of the Limit Order Book

lessons.title: Anatomy of the Limit Order Book: Bids, Asks, Depth and the Best Price

body.text: The limit order book is not a chart or a headline price. It is a live ledger of every trader's stated intent to buy or sell at a specific price, and reading it correctly tells you things no candlestick ever will.

children.text: What You Are Actually Looking At

markDefs.definition: The total resting quantity visible in the limit order book at and around the current price, usually shown as several price levels on both the bid and ask side. Depth is a direct measure of how much a stock can absorb before its price moves.

children.text: Every stock traded on the NSE or BSE has a limit order book running behind its quoted price at every instant the market is open. On one side sit bids, orders from traders willing to buy at a stated price or lower. On the other side sit asks, also called offers, orders from traders willing to sell at a stated price or higher. The highest price among all resting bids is the best bid, and the lowest price among all resting asks is the best ask. Together they define the two numbers you actually see quoted on a trading screen. Everything below the best bid and above the best ask, the full stack of orders at worse prices, is called
, and it is usually shown five, ten, or twenty levels deep on either side.

body.caption: Illustrative five-level market depth snapshot for a liquid Nifty 50 large-cap stock trading near ₹2,450

children.text: Two numbers get computed from this table constantly, by every serious market participant. The bid-ask spread is simply the best ask minus the best bid, ₹2,450.00 minus ₹2,449.95, a single tick of ₹0.05 here, since NSE's standard tick size for equities is ₹0.05. The mid price is the average of the two, the reference price this course uses throughout for measuring how good or bad an execution actually was.

body.caption: Mid price from the table above: (2,449.95 + 2,450.00) / 2 = ₹2,449.975. This is the reference point the rest of the course measures execution quality against, not the last traded price.

body.label: Best Bid-Ask Spread in This Snapshot
body.context: The minimum possible spread given NSE's ₹0.05 tick size for this price range, and exactly what a deep, actively quoted large-cap book looks like on a normal trading day.

children.text: Depth: What Sits Behind the Best Price

The best bid and best ask only tell you the price for the very first share. Depth tells you how many shares you can trade before the price has to move to the next level. In the table above, a market buy order for 2,000 shares fills entirely at ₹2,450.00, since the ask side has 2,850 shares resting there. A market buy order for 5,000 shares fills 2,850 shares at ₹2,450.00 and the remaining 2,150 shares at ₹2,450.05, walking into the second level and paying a blended average price slightly above the best ask. This is mechanical, not a forecast: the book tells you exactly what a given order size will cost, before you send it.

children.text: The Book Is Never Actually Still

A screenshot of the order book is stale the instant it is taken. On a liquid NSE large cap, thousands of new orders, modifications, and cancellations hit the book every minute, most of them from algorithmic participants operating on millisecond timescales, some of them from exchange-colocated systems reacting to the same information you are looking at. Any order book snapshot you work with, whether pulled live through a broker's depth API or reconstructed from historical tick data for a backtest, is a photograph of something that is constantly moving. Chapters 2 and 3 build directly on this fact, since it is precisely the moment-to-moment changes in the book, not any single static snapshot, that carry the most useful signal.

body.code:
def order_book_metrics(bids, asks):
    """bids/asks: list of {'price': float, 'qty': int}, unsorted."""
    best_bid = max(bids, key=lambda level: level['price'])
    best_ask = min(asks, key=lambda level: level['price'])
    mid_price = (best_bid['price'] + best_ask['price']) / 2
    spread = best_ask['price'] - best_bid['price']
    return mid_price, spread

# Illustrative depth snapshot, matching the shape most Indian broker
# market-depth APIs (e.g. Kite Connect's quote endpoint) return.
bids = [
    {'price': 2449.95, 'qty': 3200},
    {'price': 2449.90, 'qty': 5400},
]
asks = [
    {'price': 2450.00, 'qty': 2850},
    {'price': 2450.05, 'qty': 4100},
]

mid, spread = order_book_metrics(bids, asks)
print(f"Mid price: {mid:.2f}, Spread: {spread:.2f}")
# Prints the mid price (~2,449.98) and the one-tick spread (0.05)
body.caption: Computing mid price and spread from a depth snapshot. Every microstructure signal in this course starts from a function that looks close to this one.

columns.label: Deep Book (Liquid Large Cap)
points: Spread sits at one tick for most of the trading day
Thousands of shares resting within a few paise of the best price
A retail-sized order barely moves the average fill price
Cancellations and fresh orders refill the book within milliseconds

columns.label: Thin Book (Illiquid Small Cap)
points: Spread can run to tens of ticks, or more, all day
Only a few hundred shares may sit at the best price on either side
A mid-sized order can walk through several price levels
The book can stay effectively unchanged for seconds at a time

body.text: Quoted depth on your screen is not a guarantee. Resting orders can be modified or cancelled in the moments between your snapshot and your order reaching the exchange, and some large participants use iceberg orders that display only a fraction of their real size at each level. Treat displayed depth as a strong, usually reliable signal about liquidity, never as a locked-in promise of fill price.

body.title: Reading Depth Before You Click Buy
body.scenario: You are about to buy 4,000 shares of a stock. The book shows a best ask of 900 shares at ₹640.10, then 700 shares at ₹640.20, then only 250 shares at ₹640.35, then 300 shares at ₹640.60, before the ask side thickens back up to over 5,000 shares at ₹641.00.
body.prompt: If you send a single market order for the full 4,000 shares right now, roughly what will happen to your average fill price, and what does the thin patch between ₹640.35 and ₹640.60 tell you about this stock's liquidity right at this moment?
body.modelAnswer: The order walks the book level by level: 900 shares at ₹640.10, 700 at ₹640.20, 250 at ₹640.35, 300 at ₹640.60, and the remaining 1,850 shares at ₹641.00, since the book thickens up sharply there. The blended average price ends up well above the best ask of ₹640.10, and closer to ₹641.00 given how much of the order fills at that level. The thin patch between ₹640.35 and ₹640.60 shows a temporary gap in resting liquidity, exactly the kind of spot that produces a disproportionate jump in average fill price for any order large enough to reach it. Splitting the order, or waiting for the thin levels to refill, would meaningfully improve the execution.

body.title: Computing the Mid Price
body.prompt: The best bid for a stock is ₹1,842.30 and the best ask is ₹1,842.50. What is the mid price?
body.explanation: Mid price = (1,842.30 + 1,842.50) / 2 = ₹1,842.40. This is the reference price used throughout the course to measure effective spread and execution quality, not the last traded price shown on a ticker.

points: The limit order book is a live ledger of resting bids and asks at every price level, not just the single quoted price
Best bid and best ask define the top of the book; the bid-ask spread and mid price are both computed directly from them
Depth tells you how many shares trade at each price level, which is exactly what determines how much a given order size will cost
A liquid large cap typically trades with a one-tick spread and deep resting quantity; an illiquid small cap can show a spread of thirty ticks or more with thin depth
Order book snapshots are stale the instant they are captured, since orders are added, modified, and cancelled continuously
Displayed depth is a strong signal about liquidity, not a guaranteed fill price, since resting orders can vanish and iceberg orders hide their true size
